newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi wins confidence vote, rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi wins confidence vote, rate cut.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi was handed a double victory on Wednesday, winning a vote of confidence in parliament hard on the heels of a welcome discount rate cut by the central bank.
The Chamber of Deputies voted 316 to 286 for the confidence motion, which the centre-left government had called to ram into law a rescue plan for the ailing southern bank, Banco di Napoli.
The decree had been bogged down by 1,001 amendments presented by the separatist Northern League which had demanded similar state subsidies for the north.
The vote followed by four hours the Bank of Italy's unexpected decision to cut the discount rate to 7.50 percent from 8.25, citing signs that inflation was on a downward trend.
Many analysts had believed the central bank would wait to cut borrowing rates until after Prodi's deficit-cutting 1997 budget passed an initial test in parliament in mid-November.
The rate cut was welcome news to Prodi, whose government has been eager for a fall in borrowing costs to help lower the interest on Italy's huge public debt.
"It's a recognition of the validity of the work carried out by the government and a useful encouragement for the path that we still have to pursue," Prodi said.

The confidence vote was on a government decree which seeks to inject two trillion lire ($1.3 billion) of state funds into the heavily indebted Banco di Napoli and privatise it before the end of the year.
The victory swept away the filbustering amendments. A second vote will take place on Thursday on the passage into law of the decree itself, which had been set to expire on November 24.
It cannot be resurrected after that as a result of a recent Constitutional Court ruling which prevents decrees from being resubmitted.

The confidence vote was the second the government faced in parliament since taking power six months ago. Prodi won a confidence vote in August to ram a mini-budget into law, with the legislation again being threatened by League obstructionism.
Further good news for Prodi emerged on Wednesday evening when parties in his coalition appeared to have reached a deal over controversial plans to reform the income tax system.
Opposition to the tax reform had raised uncertainty about passage of Prodi's overall 1997 budget, which proposes to cut the public sector deficit by 62.5 trillion lire.
The hard-left Communist Refoundation, on whose support Prodi depends in the Chamber of Deputies, had raised concerns that changes would mean more tax for lower earners.
"There is the basis for an accord," Oliviero Diliberto, the Communist Refoundation's leader in the lower house, said after talks on Wednesday evening.
Other politicians who took part in the talks said the reform would be re-written by Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco and a senior parliamentarian.
The Chamber of Deputies will begin discussion of the budget next Wednesday. A final vote is expected by November 14.
One leader of the centre-right opposition, Gianfranco Fini, said he had asked Prodi during a meeting on Wednesday not to use any more confidence votes to push the budget through parliament.
"I asked Prodi...to guarantee parliament the chance to discuss the budget law, a law which has provoked many disputes even within the majority," Fini said.
